title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
summary: What a plateau is, the different ways plateaus form, famous examples around the world, and how plateaus differ from mountains and valleys.
poll: Living on a wide, flat plateau would be more interesting than living in a narrow valley.

versions.title: What Is a Plateau?
versions.text:
A plateau is flat land. It is high up. It is flat on top. It is not a hill. It is not a peak.

It can form in ways. Hot rock can push land up. Lava can pile up, too. The lava cools. It makes flat rock.

The edge drops down fast. The top stays flat and wide. You can walk for miles up there.

A peak is sharp. A valley is low. A plateau is flat and high. It is not sharp. It is not low.

A river can cut into it. The water cuts a deep path. We call this path a canyon. It can get very deep.

Flat high land is found all over the world. Some spots are small. Some are huge. People live on many of them.

versions.title: What Is a Plateau?
versions.text:
A plateau is a big, flat piece of land. It sits high above the land near it. It is not a hill. It is not a mountain peak. The top is wide and flat.

Plateaus form in a few ways. Hot rock deep down can push land up. This makes a high, flat spot. Some plateaus form from lava. Hot lava flows out. It spreads out flat. Then it cools into hard rock.

A plateau has steep sides. We call this the edge. The edge drops down fast. But the top stays flat. People can walk for miles up there.

A plateau is not like a mountain. A mountain has a sharp top. A plateau has a flat top. A plateau is not like a valley, too. A valley is low land. A plateau is high land.

A river can cut into a plateau. This takes many years. The water cuts a deep path. We call this path a canyon. Some canyons get very deep.

Plateaus are found all over the world. Some are small. Some stretch far. Many people live and farm on plateaus today.

versions.title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
versions.text:
A plateau is a big, flat piece of land. It sits high above the land around it. It can be as tall as a mountain. But its top is flat and wide, not sharp.

Plateaus form in a few ways. In some places, hot rock lies deep underground. It slowly pushes the land up. This makes a high, flat area over time. In other places, hot lava flows out again and again. Each layer spreads out flat. The lava cools. It turns into hard, flat rock.

A plateau usually has steep sides. We call this steep part the edge. The edge drops down fast. The top of the plateau stays mostly flat. People can walk, farm, or build towns up there.

A plateau is not the same as a mountain. A mountain has a sharp, pointed top. A plateau has a wide, flat top instead. A plateau is also not the same as a valley. A valley is low land between hills. A plateau is high land, not low land.

Over many years, a river can slowly cut into a plateau. The moving water carves out a deep path. We call this kind of path a canyon.

The Tibetan Plateau in Asia is the largest and highest plateau on Earth. Many other plateaus can be found across the world, too.

A plateau usually has steep sides. We call this part the edge. The edge drops down quickly toward the land around it. The top of the plateau stays mostly flat and level. People can walk, farm, or build towns across that flat top.

A plateau is quite different from a mountain. A mountain rises to a sharp, pointed top. A plateau keeps a wide, flat top instead. A plateau is also different from a valley. A valley is low land. It often sits between hills. A plateau is high land, not low land.

Over many years, a river can slowly cut deep into a plateau. The moving water carves out a narrow path. We call this kind of path a canyon.

The Tibetan Plateau in Asia is the largest and highest plateau on Earth. The Deccan Plateau covers much of southern India.

versions.title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
versions.text:
A plateau is a large area of land with a flat top. It sits at a high elevation, well above the land around it. A mountain usually rises to a single sharp peak. A plateau keeps a broad, level top instead.

Plateaus form in a few different ways. One process is called uplift. Forces deep underground slowly push a large block of land upward. This can take millions of years. Another process involves volcanic activity. Hot lava flows out again and again. Each new layer spreads out flat and cools. Over time, these layers build up into a thick, flat tableland.

A plateau usually has steep sides, known as its edge. The land drops quickly down to the lower ground nearby. The top of the plateau stays mostly flat and level. This is why people can farm and build towns across it.

A plateau differs from both a mountain and a valley. A mountain has a narrow, pointed summit. A plateau keeps a wide, flat top instead. A valley is low land that sits between hills. A plateau is raised land, not low land.

Rivers can slowly carve into a plateau. We call this process erosion. Over thousands of years, moving water wears away rock. It cuts a deep, narrow canyon into the flat surface.

The Tibetan Plateau in Asia is the largest and highest plateau on Earth. The Deccan Plateau covers much of southern India. The Colorado Plateau in the United States is famous for the Grand Canyon.

versions.title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
versions.text:
Plateaus are among the most striking landforms on Earth, defined by a broad, level top that sits well above the land around them. Mountains typically rise to a narrow peak, but a plateau keeps a flat, wide surface across its whole area, often large enough to support farms, towns, or even entire cities.

Geologists know of several processes that create plateaus. Tectonic uplift happens when forces deep within the earth push a large block of crust upward, sometimes over millions of years, without tilting the land very much. Volcanic plateaus form in a different way: repeated eruptions send lava flowing across the land, and each new layer cools and hardens before the next one arrives. Over time, this builds a thick, flat tableland out of many stacked layers of rock.

A plateau is usually bordered by a steep edge, often called an escarpment, where the land drops sharply down to the lower ground beyond it. This sharp boundary sets plateaus apart from the hills or plains that often surround them. Because a plateau sits at a higher elevation, its weather can also be cooler and drier than the land below.

Erosion plays an important role in shaping many plateaus over time. Rivers can slowly cut downward into the flat surface, wearing away layer after layer of rock, and over thousands or even millions of years, this process can carve a deep canyon into the land.

Several famous plateaus show this variety well. The Tibetan Plateau, often called the roof of the world, is both the largest and highest plateau on Earth, and it formed largely through tectonic uplift. The Deccan Plateau in India formed instead through huge volcanic eruptions long ago, while the Colorado Plateau in the United States is famous for the Grand Canyon, which the Colorado River carved through slow erosion over millions of years. Each plateau tells its own geologic story.

versions.title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
versions.text:
Plateaus rank among the most striking landforms on Earth, defined by a broad, level summit that rises well above the surrounding terrain; unlike mountains, which typically narrow to a single pointed peak, a plateau maintains a flat, tablelike surface across its entire area, one often large enough to support farms, towns, or even entire cities.

Geologists today recognize several distinct processes that create plateaus, each one leaving a different signature on the landscape. Tectonic uplift occurs when forces deep within the earth push an enormous block of crust upward, sometimes over millions of years, without tilting or folding the land dramatically in the process. Volcanic plateaus form quite differently: repeated eruptions send lava flowing across the land, and each successive layer cools and hardens before the next one arrives, gradually building a thick, flat tableland out of many stacked layers of rock laid down over vast stretches of geologic time.

A plateau is typically bordered by a steep edge, often called an escarpment, where the land drops sharply away toward the considerably lower ground beyond it, sometimes forming towering cliffs hundreds of meters tall; this abrupt boundary sets plateaus clearly apart from the gentler hills or plains that frequently surround them. Because a plateau sits at a much higher elevation than the land around it, its climate is often noticeably cooler and drier than that of the surrounding lowlands, a difference that can shape which plants and animals are able to survive on its surface.

Erosion also plays an especially important and lasting role in shaping many plateaus over time, as rivers slowly cut downward into the flat surface, wearing away layer after layer of rock; over thousands or even millions of years, this gradual, relentless process can carve a deep, winding canyon into what was once an unbroken expanse of flat land.

Several of the world's most famous plateaus illustrate this remarkable variety. The Tibetan Plateau, often called the roof of the world, is both the largest and highest plateau on the planet, formed largely through tectonic uplift over an immense span of geologic time. The Deccan Plateau in India instead formed through enormous volcanic eruptions long ago, while the Colorado Plateau in the western United States is famous above all for the Grand Canyon, a canyon the Colorado River carved through slow, persistent erosion over millions upon millions of years, reshaping the plateau's surface step by patient step.

versions.title: Plateaus: Earth's High Flatlands
versions.text:
Plateaus rank among the most striking landforms on Earth, defined by a broad, level summit that rises well above the surrounding terrain; unlike mountains, which typically narrow to a single pointed peak, a plateau maintains a flat, tablelike surface across its entire area, one frequently large enough to support farms, towns, or even entire cities built directly atop it.

Geologists recognize several distinct geologic processes that create plateaus, each one leaving a markedly different signature on the surrounding landscape. Tectonic uplift occurs when forces deep within the earth push an enormous block of crust upward, sometimes over millions of years, without tilting or folding the overlying land dramatically in the process. Volcanic plateaus form quite differently: repeated eruptions send lava flowing extensively across the land, and each successive layer cools and hardens before the next one arrives, gradually building a thick, flat tableland out of countless stacked layers of rock laid down over vast, almost unimaginable stretches of geologic time.

A plateau is typically bordered by a steep edge, often termed an escarpment, where the land drops sharply away toward the considerably lower ground beyond it, at times forming towering cliffs hundreds of meters tall; this abrupt boundary sets plateaus unmistakably apart from the gentler hills or plains that frequently surround them. Because a plateau sits at a substantially higher elevation than the land around it, its climate is often markedly cooler and drier than that of the surrounding lowlands, a difference that can profoundly shape which plants and animals are able to survive on its exposed surface.

Erosion plays an especially significant role in shaping many plateaus over time, as rivers slowly and persistently cut downward into the flat surface, wearing away layer after layer of ancient rock; over thousands or even millions of years, this gradual, relentless process can carve a deep, winding canyon into what was once an unbroken expanse of flat, elevated land.

Several of the world's most famous plateaus illustrate this remarkable geologic variety. The Tibetan Plateau, often called the roof of the world, is both the largest and highest plateau on the entire planet, formed largely through tectonic uplift over an immense, almost incomprehensible span of geologic time. The Deccan Plateau in India instead formed through a series of enormous volcanic eruptions long ago, while the Colorado Plateau in the western United States is famous above all else for the Grand Canyon, a canyon the Colorado River carved through slow, persistent erosion over millions upon millions of years of patient, continuous geologic work that reshaped the plateau's surface step by step.

MID.prompt: Explain two different ways that a plateau can form, using details from the article.
checklist: I named two ways a plateau can form.
I used details from the article to explain each way.
MID.modelAnswer: A plateau can form through uplift, when forces deep underground slowly push a large block of land upward over millions of years. A plateau can also form from repeated volcanic eruptions, when layer after layer of lava spreads out, cools, and hardens until a thick tableland builds up. Both processes create the same kind of wide, flat landform, even though they happen in very different ways.

HIGH.prompt: Compare how tectonic uplift and volcanic activity each create a plateau, and explain how erosion can later reshape that same plateau. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained how tectonic uplift creates a plateau.
I explained how volcanic activity creates a plateau.
I explained how erosion can later reshape a plateau, using evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A plateau formed by tectonic uplift rises when forces deep within the earth slowly push a large block of crust upward over millions of years, as described for the Tibetan Plateau. A plateau formed by volcanic activity, like the Deccan Plateau, instead builds up gradually as repeated lava eruptions cool into stacked layers of rock that harden into a thick tableland. Once a plateau exists, erosion can still reshape it: as the Colorado Plateau shows, a river can slowly wear away layer after layer of rock over millions of years, eventually carving a deep canyon like the Grand Canyon into what was once an unbroken, flat surface.
